verdicts.evidence: [FACT] KOLD, Oct. 30, 2026: PCSD "continues to work our labs in hopes of furthering our DNA analysis"; she is still missing. Parade via Yahoo, Oct. 31: "no arrests made", no suspect named. The only arrest (Luke Daley, booked Sept. 30) was "unrelated to the Nancy Guthrie case" (PCSD via Men's Journal, Oct. 6). Through Nov. 11 I found no report that she has been found or anyone charged, so the claim is still accurate as dated.

[FACT] NBC News: Patel wrote on X: "The video was recovered from residual data located in backend systems". The page's quoted fragment is verbatim and attributed to the right person. Google "was assisting with the Guthrie investigation and could not provide further details". NPR (Feb. 12) quotes the same words.
verdicts.source_read: https://www.nbcnewyork.com/news/national-international/nancy-guthrie-google-nest-camera-video-from-backend-systems/6459531/ (NBC News, Feb. 10, 2026; nbcnews.com itself blocked to the fetcher) ; https://www.npr.org/2026/02/12/nx-s1-5711620/nancy-guthrie-video-footage-fbi

verdicts.evidence: [REASONING] Labeled as inference, and it claims nothing it can't back. Both possibilities are real. Google support says a Nest device without a subscription keeps "Up to 3 hours of event video history" (some models up to 6 hours of previews). Note: the footage was released on Feb. 10, about nine days later, and was described as "residual" data. That retrieval falls outside a 3-hour window either way, so the line saying the first case 'would mean the plan was misunderstood' is weaker than it reads. This does not block.
verdicts.source_read: https://support.google.com/googlehome/answer/9681538?hl=en ; https://www.nbcnewyork.com/news/national-international/nancy-guthrie-google-nest-camera-video-from-backend-systems/6459531/ (NBC News, Feb. 10, 2026; nbcnews.com itself blocked to the fetcher)

verdicts.evidence: [FACT] USAO-DC, 48-month update (Jan. 2025): "Approximately 1,583 defendants have been federally charged". That covers Jan. 2021 to Jan. 2025, so 'more than 1,500 over four years' is right. The REPORTED tag is weaker than needed but acceptable.

[FACT] The 'one input among many' half is supported: IEEE Spectrum (Mark Harris, Jan. 5, 2024) says 63% of suspects were first named by witnesses through 2022, and other cases came from facial recognition. The absence half is overstated. Reporting by the same journalist is public: IEEE Spectrum says "fewer than 200 people have been charged using that information". The Wired piece the page lists as a source (Nov. 2022, read via a mirror because wired.com was blocked) says geofence evidence was cited in over 100 charging documents and gave the initial identification in nearly 50 cases. Also an extractor artifact: the ledger text begins with the previous tag word.
verdicts.fix: The geofence return was one input among many, alongside video, tips and social media; no official count exists, but reporting by IEEE Spectrum found fewer than 200 people had been charged using the geofence data by January 2024. INFERENCE

verdicts.evidence: [FACT] The proclamation (DCPD-202500112) commutes 14 named sentences and pardons "all other individuals convicted". It gives no count, and it orders dismissal of "all pending indictments"; those people were not pardoned. DOJ counted about 1,230 convicted on Jan. 3, 2025 (1,009 guilty pleas plus 221 trial verdicts). The figure 'about 1,500' comes only from press reports (e.g. CBS: 'Trump pardons about 1,500 Jan. 6 defendants'), so a FACT tag certifies a number the primary document does not contain.
verdicts.fix: On Jan. 20, 2025, President Trump commuted 14 sentences, pardoned everyone else convicted, and ordered pending cases dismissed; news reports put the total granted clemency at about 1,500. REPORTED

verdicts.evidence: [FACT] Stat card '~30,000 WMATA cameras across trains, buses, stations, and power systems'. WMATA (Feb. 21, 2024): "more than 30,000 cameras on buses, trains, and in stations". NBC4 (Aug. 6, 2024): "trains, buses, stations and their power systems, with about 30,000 cameras".

[FACT] Stat card '~1,300 MPD CCTV cameras'. No source gives 1,300. The page cites none, and MPD's CCTV policy page has no count. The latest MPD figures I found: "199 cameras" (Nov. 2019 announcement) and "about 300 cameras" (MPD's Smith, DCist, Dec. 7, 2023). GovTech (Aug. 2025) gives only the RTCC's combined "more than 28,000 public and private cameras". The number may have grown since 2023, but nothing I read supports 1,300.
verdicts.fix: Cite a current MPD count with its date, or drop the card. The last public figure we found was about 300 MPD-owned cameras (Dec. 2023).

verdicts.evidence: [FACT] Stat card '~2,500 sites ... CameraConnect / Capital Shield, shared to MPD via Kastle'. Kastle/MPD (Apr. 2024): CapitalShield "has expanded to more than 1,000 locations", plus 1,000 donated cameras (that is cameras, not sites). No 2,500 figure found. The card also merges two programs: CameraConnect DC is MPD's camera registry for residents and businesses, with no Kastle link, and Capital Shield is the Kastle partnership with commercial owners.
verdicts.fix: 1,000+ locations in Capital Shield, a Kastle and MPD partnership with commercial property owners (Kastle, April 2024). Residents' registered cameras (CameraConnect DC) are a separate registry.

verdicts.evidence: [FACT] Stat card '30 days default Flock LPR retention' (also the Flock lane in Exhibit B and defense 04). Flock's LPR policy, last updated June 30, 2026: "LPR data is hard deleted on a rolling 7-day basis by default". Police1 (Aug. 14, 2026) reports Flock cut its recommended default "from 30 days to seven". In D.C. itself, NOTUS (Aug. 28, 2026) reports MPD keeps Flock data "for up to three months". The 'AWS GovCloud' part is supported: data is "transferred to the AWS Government Cloud".
verdicts.fix: Flock's default retention is now 7 days (cut from 30 in 2026), but D.C. police keep their Flock plate data for up to three months (NOTUS, Aug. 2026). Stored in AWS's government cloud.

verdicts.evidence: [FACT] Stat card '9,000+ bldgs, federal facilities protected by DHS/FPS, many with continuous CCTV'. DHS: "9,000 federal government buildings across the US". GAO-23-105361: "about 9,000". The '+' is not in either source. The figure is nationwide, but the card sits in a D.C. strip without saying so (Standard s.1). 'Many with continuous CCTV' is not in any source I read.
verdicts.fix: About 9,000 federal facilities nationwide, not D.C. alone, are protected by DHS's Federal Protective Service.

verdicts.evidence: [FACT] Stat card '90 days standard MPD CCTV retention'. MPD: "Generally, video recordings are maintained by the MPDC for a maximum of 90 calendar days before being purged" unless needed for a criminal or administrative investigation, and "Video is retained based on incident type and relevant statutes of limitation." The 2011 MPD fact sheet also lists civil liability as an exception. Note: MPD calls 90 days a maximum; the page calls it standard.

[FACT] The 'training' exception to MPD's 90-day CCTV retention (stat card and MPD lane hover). It is not in MPD's CCTV policy page or the 2011 fact sheet. The governing regulation, 24 DCMR 2505, may contain it, but I could not read it: the proxy rejected the cloudfront copy and I found no other copy.

[FRAME] The Exhibit A lead says 'a callout shows how many cameras are in that block'. The callout prints 'N cameras in this block' with a 'MPD n, WMTA n, FED n, PRIV n, LPR n' breakdown. The legend says 'cameras within ~500 ft' and the tally counts 'cams'. In the script, every one of these numbers is Math.round of a distance-weighted sum over hand-placed HOT seed weights. They are not camera counts. That contradicts the same lead ('not a block-by-block count') and the Nov. 11 correction, which removed Exhibit F because its 'camera count described nothing real'. Exhibit A still does the same thing.
verdicts.source_read: episode-05-the-replayable-city.html (lead line 760; legend line 1033; script HOT/computeAtCell/fireHexCallout lines 1500-1543, 1744-1756)
verdicts.fix: Replace the numeric callout and the 'cams' tally with a relative density band (Low/Moderate/High/Very high) labeled 'editorial model, illustrative'. Change the legend to 'relative density (illustrative)'.

verdicts.evidence: [FRAME] The running tally's 'Speed reads' adds 1 for every VDOT, NPS, MoCo, PG or DDOT pin. The script comment says these 'are speed/traffic enforcement', but VDOT and NPS camera pins are not shown to be speed enforcement anywhere. The 'Classified presence' layer puts the same six pins (JBAB, USPP, FBI, SS, CAPITOL, SFRA) at fixed fractions of every route, whatever the geography; JBAB appears on the Falls Church route, for example. Nothing labels these as illustrative, and the lead says the tally 'counts every kind of read the architecture takes from you, in real time.'
verdicts.fix: Label the tally and the classified layer 'illustrative, not measured', and drop the claim that it counts every read.

verdicts.evidence: [FACT] Layer buttons say 'FAA FRZ · 15 mi' and 'FAA SFRA · 30 mi'. FAA: SFRA is "a 30 nautical mile (about 33 statute miles) radius", and the FRZ "extends approximately 15 nautical miles (about 17 statute miles)". The unit is wrong.
verdicts.fix: FAA FRZ · 15 nm ; FAA SFRA · 30 nm

verdicts.evidence: [FACT] Exhibit A says 'the routes are real roads' and offers 'Choose a commute · 40 min each'. Route r1 is listed as 'Georgia Ave · 14th St · S Capitol', but its turn list says 'Head S on Georgia Ave NW' then 'Continue on 16th St NW'. Georgia Avenue does not continue into 16th Street, and the turn list never uses 14th St. Drive times in the data are 38, 40, 42 and 40 minutes, not 40 each.
verdicts.fix: Make the r1 turn list match a real path (e.g. Georgia Ave to 7th St NW), and say 'about 40 min each'.

verdicts.evidence: [FRAME] Every 'Residual tail: up to X' value in the hover (MPD 5 yrs, WMATA 2 yrs, DDOT 18 mo, Flock 3 yrs, FPS 5 yrs, USPP 5 yrs, USSS 5 yrs, Capital Shield 90 d, doorbell 3 yrs) and the striped bars are unsourced. The page's own method note says the cross-system tail is something 'no public source measures'. These are Infera's model values shown as measurements, with no 'editorial model' label (Standard s.3). MPD does say footage is kept per 'statutes of limitation', which supports a tail existing but not its length.
verdicts.fix: Label the residual bars 'editorial model, illustrative' and show them as bands ('can extend for the life of a case'), not 'up to N years'.

verdicts.evidence: [FACT] Official retention values in the lanes. Checked and supported: WMATA 90 d (NBC4: Metro "usually stores video footage for 90 days"), USPP 180 d (GAO-03-748: "no more than 6 months"; NPS schedule: 6 months), doorbell 60 d (Ring: default "60 days for 1080p and 2K devices", 30 for 4K). No source found: DDOT 60 d, FPS 120 d, FPS 'Continuous CCTV on most', and USSS 'Treat as continuous, indefinite', which is speculation phrased as an instruction. Flock 30 d is p004; Capital Shield 2 d is p014.
verdicts.fix: Source DDOT and FPS retention or mark them 'not published'. Replace the USSS line with 'Retention not publicly documented.'

verdicts.evidence: [QUOTE] USPP hover: 'Mall planning documents described a system "not to exceed five years."' I could not find this phrase. GAO-03-748 says USPP recordings "are to be retained for no more than 6 months and then destroyed unless needed as evidence"; its only 'not to exceed' is a D.C. pilot bill ('not to exceed 1 year'). The NPS records schedule N1-079-08-002 gives CCTV '6 months'. The quotation cannot be presented as verbatim without a document.
verdicts.fix: U.S. Park Police policy keeps recordings no more than six months unless they are needed as evidence (GAO, 2003).

verdicts.evidence: [FACT] The page merges two programs. Capital Shield lane: 'Rebate program requires at least 48-hour retention.' Defense 03: 'D.C. residents opted into the Capital Shield program through a published rebate.' Defense 04: 'private rebate 48 hours' listed as a finite retention window. In fact the 48-hour rule belongs to OVSJG's Private Security Camera Rebate Program: applicants must prove cameras can "retain at least forty-eight (48) hours of video footage". That is a minimum, not a limit, and those participants "are required to register their cameras with the MPD". Capital Shield is "a public/private video sharing partnership between the MPD, Kastle Systems Security, and local businesses", with cameras donated by Kastle. No source mentions a rebate for it.
verdicts.fix: Defense 03: 'Thousands of D.C. residents installed cameras through a city rebate program that requires registering them with MPD.' Defense 04: drop '48 hours' from the list of limits (it is a minimum). Lane: split into 'Capital Shield (Kastle, commercial)' and 'Rebate cameras (at least 48 hours, MPD may request footage)'.

verdicts.evidence: [FACT] The 'FOIA-able' cells. MPD 'Heavy Exemption 7 redactions': MPD falls under D.C. FOIA, whose law-enforcement exemption is "Investigatory records compiled for law enforcement purposes" (D.C. Code 2-534(a)(3)), not federal Exemption 7. WMATA 'Limited release; safety-incident only': WMATA is not under FOIA; it uses its PARP plus an External Video Request Form, and body-camera footage can be released to subjects. Nothing limits release to safety incidents. USSS 'Categorically denied': no source found.
verdicts.fix: MPD: 'D.C. FOIA; law-enforcement exemption often applied'. WMATA: 'Not under FOIA; request through Metro's records policy or its video request form'. USSS: 'Subject to FOIA; protective records usually withheld' (cite the source or remove).

verdicts.evidence: [FACT] Flock lane 'Who can preserve: Any law-enforcement agency with vendor access'. In D.C., MPD grants outside requests, federal ones included, "on a case-by-case basis" (Interim Chief Carroll via NOTUS). One-step national access is not the D.C. setup.
verdicts.fix: MPD, and other agencies MPD approves case by case.

verdicts.evidence: [FACT] Guthrie anchor, untagged parts. Headline 'without a paid plan still yielded video': NPR has Nanos saying the camera "wasn't connected to a paid subscription". NBC paraphrases him as saying she "did not have a subscription that would have saved video", and the page uses no quote marks there, which is correct. 'In February 2026 ... 84-year-old ... taken from her Tucson home': last seen Jan. 31, removed early Feb. 1 from the Catalina Foothills near Tucson; the sheriff treats it as a kidnapping. The NBC disclosure is present and adjacent. The sources line matches what I read.
verdicts.source_read: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Disappearance_of_Nancy_Guthrie ; https://www.npr.org/2026/02/12/nx-s1-5711620/nancy-guthrie-video-footage-fbi ; https://www.nbcnewyork.com/news/national-international/nancy-guthrie-google-nest-camera-video-from-backend-systems/6459531/ (NBC News, Feb. 10, 2026; nbcnews.com itself blocked to the fetcher)

verdicts.evidence: [FACT] Data-debt bullet: 'Residual backend data. The Guthrie precedent. Footage believed deleted is recoverable from system logs.' Patel said "residual data located in backend systems"; nothing says 'system logs'. One case is stated as a general rule. It also contradicts the retrofitted anchor, which now says 'What we do not know'. The doorbell lane's 'may persist ... (see Guthrie precedent)' is acceptably hedged.
verdicts.source_read: https://www.nbcnewyork.com/news/national-international/nancy-guthrie-google-nest-camera-video-from-backend-systems/6459531/ (NBC News, Feb. 10, 2026; nbcnews.com itself blocked to the fetcher)
verdicts.fix: Residual backend data. In the Guthrie case the FBI recovered video from a camera without a paid plan from 'residual data located in backend systems'; how long such data persists is not public.

verdicts.evidence: [FACT] 'The FBI's January 2021 geofence warrant required Google to identify every Android device inside a precise Capitol-grounds polygon.' The government's filing in U.S. v. Rhine (ECF 59) says the warrant, issued Jan. 13, 2021, sought "certain Location History information for devices that connected to its services from a specific geographic area corresponding approximately to the U.S. Capitol Building". That is Google Location History accounts, which were off by default (Wired), not every Android device, and the area was the building, not the grounds (Lawfare: it 'closely contour[ed] the Capitol building itself'). 'January 2021' and '5,723' are supported (Rhine opinion via Lawfare: 5,723 unique devices).
verdicts.fix: The FBI's January 2021 geofence warrant required Google to identify devices with Location History turned on inside an area drawn around the Capitol building during the breach window.

verdicts.evidence: [FACT] 'Those identifiers were narrowed against subscriber data, cell-tower handshakes, social-media posts, facial-recognition matches against driver's-license photos, employer records, and ... tips.' The court record narrows the 5,723 by removing devices seen in control windows (about 1,498 plus 37 = 1,535) and then obtains subscriber information. Tower data, facial recognition (reference images include "state driver's license pictures") and tips were separate investigative tools (IEEE Spectrum), not a narrowing of the geofence list. 'Employer records': no source found.
verdicts.fix: Investigators narrowed the list by removing devices also present before and after the breach, then obtained subscriber details for about 1,535. Separately, they used tower data, facial recognition against passport and driver's-license photos, social media and public tips.

verdicts.evidence: [FRAME] The lead calls the breach 'the proof of concept for everything in the instant replay', and the funnel draws 5,723 devices narrowing to 1,500+ charged and then ~1,500 pardoned. A funnel shows a subset, so it implies the charged came out of the geofence return. The small label 'many sources' does not undo that. Reporting puts geofence-based charges at fewer than 200 (IEEE Spectrum), and two of the three bars measure different things (charges, then clemency).
verdicts.fix: Draw three separate bars, not a funnel: '5,723 devices in the geofence return', '~1,583 people charged from many sources (fewer than 200 using geofence data, per reporting)', '14 commuted, the rest pardoned or dismissed'. Change 'proof of concept for everything' to 'an early large-scale example'.

verdicts.evidence: [FACT] 'The records outlived the prosecutions.' This is untagged and the page gives no source on what happened to the geofence returns, subscriber records or case files after the January 2025 pardons and dismissals.
verdicts.fix: Cite a source showing the records still exist, or tag it as INFERENCE: 'The pardons ended the prosecutions; nothing we found says the collected records were destroyed.'

verdicts.evidence: [FACT] Footer: 'charging and pardon totals from Justice Department and White House records.' The proclamation has no pardon total (see c006). The ~1,500 figure comes from news reports.
verdicts.fix: ...the charging total from Justice Department records and the clemency figure from news reports of the Jan. 20, 2025 proclamation.

verdicts.evidence: [QUOTE] Step 3 puts '"Records compiled for law enforcement purposes"' in quote marks. Exemption 7 reads "records or information compiled for law enforcement purposes" (5 U.S.C. 552(b)(7), as amended in 1986; DOJ OIP Guide). The quotation drops 'or information', so it is not verbatim. The 7(A)-7(F) range is right.
verdicts.fix: "Records or information compiled for law enforcement purposes" lets the agency withhold...

verdicts.evidence: [FACT] FOIA timing. Supported: 20 working days (federal), and the requester gets at least 90 days to appeal (OIP: "a minimum of 90 days"). Not supported: 'a 30 to 120-day actual response' (no source), and 'Appeal panel review takes another 20 to 60 working days'. OIP says appeals are to be decided "within twenty working-days" absent unusual circumstances, and gives no 60-day figure or 'panel'.
verdicts.fix: Statute: 20 working days to decide an appeal, with extensions in unusual circumstances; actual times vary by agency (see its annual FOIA report).

verdicts.evidence: [FRAME] Exhibit D lays out federal FOIA only (20 working days, Exemption 7, a lawsuit under 552(a)(4)(B) in federal district court). Its cited sources include 'MPD FOIA practice' and it asks whether 'the history of you' is FOIA-able. But MPD and DDOT footage falls under D.C. FOIA: 15 business days (25 for body-camera video), appeal to the Mayor or D.C. Superior Court, D.C.'s own law-enforcement exemption. WMATA is under neither law; it uses its PARP and video request form. Private and Capital Shield cameras are outside FOIA altogether. Most of the cameras on this page do not travel this path.
verdicts.fix: Retitle the pipeline 'For federal cameras (FPS, Park Police, Secret Service)' and add a short D.C. column: 15 business days, appeal to the Mayor or Superior Court; WMATA by its own records policy; private cameras not covered.

verdicts.evidence: [FACT] Exhibit D lead: surveillance footage is 'the longest, slowest, and most denied category of public-records request', and 'The pipeline below is the one most requests actually travel.' These are superlatives with no source; step 3 itself says 'we found no national count'.
verdicts.fix: In practice, requests for surveillance footage are often slow and often withheld under law-enforcement exemptions; we found no national count.

verdicts.evidence: [FRAME] Exhibit E: 'In practice, the curve has a long, fat tail'. The 'actual practice' curve has a 0-100% 'SHARE STILL RETRIEVABLE' axis, and the text ends with 'the difference between a 90-day retention policy and a 5-year recoverable history'. Nothing measures this; the method note says the exceptions add up across systems in a way 'which no public source measures'. A drawn curve on a percentage axis implies measurement (Standard s.3).
verdicts.fix: Label the chart 'editorial model, illustrative; no public data measures this', drop the percentage ticks, and say 'a policy of 90 days and a history that can last as long as a case does'.

verdicts.evidence: [FACT] 'Criminal investigation. Preserved on request, no statutory ceiling.' For data held by a provider (Ring, Google, cloud vendors), 18 U.S.C. 2703(f)(2) says preserved records "shall be retained for a period of 90 days", extended "for an additional 90-day period upon a renewed request". That is a ceiling on preservation without a court order. No statute caps agencies' own evidence.
verdicts.fix: Criminal investigation. Agencies keep evidence for the life of a case; a preservation request to a vendor holds data for 90 days, renewable once, pending a court order.

verdicts.evidence: [FACT] The other 'Why the tail' lines are stated as universal rules: 'The exceptions named on every retention policy are not edge cases'; 'Litigation hold. Any open case freezes related footage indefinitely'; 'Vendor backups ... often distinct from contract'; 'Contractor archives. Maintenance and integration vendors keep their own copies.' The page gives no source for any of them. MPD's policy supports only retention 'based on incident type and relevant statutes of limitation'.
verdicts.fix: Litigation hold: footage related to a case is kept until the case ends. Vendor backups and contractor copies: 'can exist; their retention is rarely published.'

verdicts.evidence: [REASONING] Defense 05 says WMATA cameras 'have been cited in arrests', which is supported: WMATA says images "are often used by MTPD and other local law enforcement agencies to identify suspects and make arrests". Fare-evasion and missing-person uses were not found. The rebuttal, 'no oversight body that maps across all 30,000 sources', treats WMATA's camera count as the size of the whole system of systems. The RTCC network alone is "more than 28,000 public and private cameras" (GovTech), separate from WMATA's.
verdicts.fix: True. No single body oversees Metro's 30,000-plus cameras together with police, federal and private networks, or the agencies that can pull from them.

verdicts.evidence: [REASONING] Defense 06 rebuttal: 'Exemption 7 is also the reason the camera that watched you almost never produces a record you can review.' 'Almost never' has no number, the page itself found 'no national count', and most cameras on the page are not under federal FOIA at all (p026). Private cameras produce nothing through FOIA for a different reason: they are private.
verdicts.fix: Law-enforcement exemptions, and the fact that private cameras sit outside public-records law, mean the camera that watched you often produces no record you can get.

verdicts.evidence: [REASONING] Defense 02 rebuttal: 'Public-space doctrine assumes the watched can identify the watcher and adjust behavior.' The doctrine does not rest on that premise. The real counter is aggregation: long-term tracking of a person's whole movements can be a search (the Fourth Circuit en banc in Leaders of a Beautiful Struggle v. Baltimore, 2021, building on Carpenter, 2018). The other side is fairly stated; the answer to it is not.
verdicts.source_read: https://www.aclu.org/press-releases/federal-appeals-court-rules-baltimore-aerial-surveillance-program-unconstitutional (search result; Brennan Center and Harvard Law Review summaries)
verdicts.fix: Courts have started to treat the aggregate differently: in 2021 a federal appeals court held that Baltimore's citywide aerial tracking was a search. Many networks sharing one view raise the same question.

verdicts.evidence: [FACT] Defense 01: 'dozens of foreign embassies'. NCPC (2019): "approximately 185 countries operating foreign missions" in Washington. That understates the other side's own case.
verdicts.fix: ...more than 170 foreign embassies...

verdicts.evidence: [FRAME] Deck and meta description: 'the data debt many Americans have but very few could account for until now.' 'Many' and 'very few' are scale words with no numbers. 'Until now' claims the page lets readers account for their data debt, but its numbers are illustrative (p008, p011, p028) and it covers D.C. only.
verdicts.fix: Then the part nobody photographs: retention math, and a data debt that no one has measured.

verdicts.evidence: [FACT] Correction note, Nov. 11. What it lists matches the diff of commit 05c7913: the old text did say 'A real forty-minute Washington commute' and 'NPR · FBI affidavit reporting', the old funnel did show '1,535 named individuals', and Exhibit F was removed. But (a) it says 'the density cells show a pattern, not a measured count', and the cells still print camera counts (p008); (b) it says '1,300 charged', where the old text said '1,300 federal charges' (charges, not people); (c) it leaves out substantive changes that soften factual claims: 'Most surveillance-footage requests land here', 'Most appeals affirm the original determination', 'the path where most successful releases happen', 'Most members of the public have none of those', the marquee 'the footage was archived', and the anchor's 'Verified anchor ... the proof that "residual" is real' and 'reported missing'.
verdicts.fix: Add: 'Exhibit D said most footage requests are denied, most appeals fail and most releases come through litigation; we found no counts and now say often or many. A pull quote said footage "was archived"; it now says exceptions can keep it.' Fix the callouts before the note says they show a pattern.

verdicts.evidence: [FACT] Method note: 'retention figures rest on each operator's published policy; counts of cameras on operator statements, labeled where single-source.' The residual retention figures rest on no policy (p011). The MPD and Capital Shield counts match no operator statement I found (p002, p003). No camera count on the page carries a single-source label.
verdicts.fix: Official retention figures rest on published policy where we found one; residual figures are an editorial model; camera counts are cited in each card with date and source.

verdicts.evidence: [FACT] Footer: 'Density cells are illustrative of pattern, anchored to documented infrastructure (MPD CCTV policy, WMATA reporting, Capital Shield documentation, Flock published policy, GSA/FPS records).' The cells come from 66 hand-placed seed points with invented weights and radii in the script. None of the named sources gives camera locations or densities at that grain; MPD's CCTV policy page gives no count at all.
verdicts.fix: Density cells are an editorial model of where camera networks concentrate (federal core, Metro hubs, commercial corridors); they are not drawn from camera-location data.

flags: EDITORIAL STANDARD, conflict note: missing. Google is a subject (the Nest backend in the Guthrie anchor, the Jan. 6 geofence, the Nest lane) and so is Amazon (Ring lane and pins, AWS GovCloud for Flock). Both are investors in or competitors of Anthropic. The site's precedent (same-model-different-customer.html) carries the note when Amazon and Google appear. Neither the page nor this verdict can certify independence: the page was retrofitted by Claude, and this checker is also Claude, made by Anthropic.

EDITORIAL STANDARD, other side: present and real (six defenses). But two of them misstate the facts (defense 03 rebate/Capital Shield, defense 04 '48 hours' as a limit: p014), one undersells the other side (p034), and three rebuttals overreach (p031-p033).

EDITORIAL STANDARD, s.7 and s.1: the page has no 'At a glance' guide (no exhibit-guide.css or js) and no 'where Infera stands' line. Stat cards do not name their scope (FPS is nationwide; the Flock default is not D.C.'s setting).

LEVEL 3, Guthrie passage: the quote is verbatim and correctly attributed to Patel's X post as reported by NBC News; the sheriff's statement is paraphrased without quote marks, which is correct; the case status is accurate as of Oct. 30 and still open as of Nov. 11 (no recovery or kidnapping arrest found). The NBC disclosure is present beside the passage. The only Guthrie problem left is outside the anchor: p018 ('system logs', stated as a rule).

LEDGER: the extractor tagged only 6 claims; the remaining 39 verdicts (p001-p039) cover untagged prose, stat cards, script data and notes, as the editor asked. Extractor artifact: c005 and c006 claim text begins with the previous tag word ('REPORTED', 'INFERENCE'); the tags themselves were read correctly.
